options.a: 1) Act with integrity, competence, diligence, respect. 2) Place client interests above personal. 3) Use reasonable care and judgment. 4) Practice independently and objectively. 5) Promote integrity of capital markets.
options.b: A) Disclosure of conflicts: disclose actual and potential conflicts. B) Priority of transactions: clients before employer before personal. C) Referral fees: disclose referral arrangements to clients.
options.c: A) Knowledge of law: comply with most strict applicable law. B) Independence: avoid conflicts, disclose if unavoidable. C) Misrepresentation: no false statements. D) Misconduct: no fraud or dishonesty.
options.d: 1) Act with integrity and respect. 2) Place employer interests above client interests. 3) Use reasonable care and judgment. 4) Comply with local law even where it is less strict. 5) Promote integrity of capital markets.

distractorExplanations.d: Reverses two core rules: the Code puts client interests and the profession above the employer's, and members must follow the stricter of local law or the Code and Standards.
distractorExplanations.b: Disclosure doesn't eliminate conflict — but makes it manageable. Family member's account: treat same as any client (no front-running).
distractorExplanations.c: 'Most strict' — not just local law. CFA Standards may be stricter than local law → must follow CFA Standards.

options.a: 1) Act with integrity, competence, diligence, respect. 2) Place client interests above personal. 3) Use reasonable care and judgment. 4) Practice independently and objectively. 5) Promote integrity of capital markets.
options.b: A) Loyalty, prudence, care: act in client's best interest. B) Fair dealing: treat all clients fairly. C) Suitability: recommendations suitable for specific client. D) Performance presentation: fair, accurate, complete.
options.c: A) Diligence and reasonable basis: have adequate basis for recommendations. B) Communication: disclose limitations and risks. C) Record retention: maintain records supporting analysis (7 years recommended).
options.d: A) Loyalty to employer: put the firm's interest ahead of clients. B) Fair dealing: give every client identical service levels. C) Suitability: one model allocation for all clients. D) Performance: show best-performing accounts.

distractorExplanations.d: Distorts Standard III: loyalty is owed to clients first, fair dealing allows different service levels if disclosed, suitability is client-specific, and cherry-picking accounts violates III(D).
distractorExplanations.a: Code is broad principles. Standards of Professional Conduct provide specific guidance. Both apply to all CFA members and candidates globally.
distractorExplanations.c: Distinguish fact from opinion. 'Company will earn $2/share' = opinion, not fact. Must be clearly labeled. 7-year record retention is a recommendation, not requirement.

options.a: A) Loyalty: act in employer's interest even above client interests. B) Additional compensation: oral notice to the employer is enough for outside work. C) Responsibilities of supervisors: supervise just the staff who hold CFA membership.
options.b: A) Loyalty, prudence, care: act in client's best interest. B) Fair dealing: treat all clients fairly. C) Suitability: recommendations suitable for specific client. D) Performance presentation: fair, accurate, complete.
options.c: A) Loyalty: act in employer's interest, don't harm employer. B) Additional compensation: get written consent for outside compensation arrangements. C) Responsibilities of supervisors: prevent ethics violations by supervised staff.
options.d: A) Disclosure of conflicts: disclose actual and potential conflicts. B) Priority of transactions: clients before employer before personal. C) Referral fees: disclose referral arrangements to clients.

distractorExplanations.a: Misstates Standard IV: employer loyalty never overrides duty to clients, IV(B) requires written consent from all parties, and supervisors are responsible for all staff they supervise, not just CFA members.
distractorExplanations.b: Soft dollars: using client brokerage to pay for research = acceptable IF benefits clients. Using for personal items = violation.
distractorExplanations.d: Disclosure doesn't eliminate conflict — but makes it manageable. Family member's account: treat same as any client (no front-running).

options.a: Excess return per unit of systematic risk (beta).
options.b: Return above the CAPM required return given the portfolio's beta.
options.c: Excess return per unit of total risk (standard deviation).
options.d: Active return per unit of tracking error versus the benchmark.

distractorExplanations.a: Excess return per unit of beta is the Treynor ratio; the Sharpe ratio divides by total risk (standard deviation).
distractorExplanations.b: Return above the CAPM required return is Jensen's alpha, an absolute measure, not a return-per-unit-of-risk ratio.
distractorExplanations.d: Active return divided by tracking error is the information ratio, which measures active management versus a benchmark.

cfa-level-1-readiness-check-010.explanation: Excess return per unit of total risk (standard deviation). Higher = better risk-adjusted performance. Formula: $$SR = \frac{\bar{R}_p - R_f}{\sigma_p}$$ Example: Portfolio return 12%, risk-free 3%, std dev 15% → SR = (12-3)/15 = 0.60. Higher = better risk-adjusted performance.

options.a: Fiscal tools: government spending levels, tax rates, transfer payments, and deficit financing through bond issuance — set by the legislature and treasury to manage aggregate demand.
options.b: Policy rate (fed funds rate / repo rate): primary tool. Reserve requirements: % of deposits banks must hold. Open market operations: buy/sell government bonds. Forward guidance: communication of future policy.
options.c: Policy rate: primary tool. Reserve requirements: % of deposits banks must hold. Exchange-rate pegs: fixed by the treasury. Tariffs and import quotas: used by the central bank to control domestic inflation.
options.d: Policy rate: primary tool. Open market operations: selling bonds to expand the money supply. Reserve requirements: raising them to stimulate lending. Forward guidance: a binding legal commitment on future rates.

distractorExplanations.a: Spending, taxes, and transfers are fiscal policy tools controlled by government, not monetary policy tools used by the central bank.
distractorExplanations.c: Tariffs, quotas, and treasury-set pegs are trade or government tools; the central bank's tools are the policy rate, reserve requirements, OMO, and guidance.
distractorExplanations.d: Gets the directions wrong: selling bonds drains reserves (contractionary), raising reserve requirements restricts lending, and forward guidance is communication, not a binding commitment.

options.a: LIFO: allowed IFRS, prohibited US GAAP. Inventory write-down reversal: allowed US GAAP, prohibited IFRS. Development costs: expensed IFRS, capitalized US GAAP. Investment property fair value: US GAAP option.
options.b: LIFO: allowed under both. Inventory write-down reversal: prohibited under both. Development costs: expensed under both. Investment property: historical cost only under both, as the two frameworks have converged.
options.c: LIFO: allowed US GAAP, prohibited IFRS. Inventory write-down reversal: allowed IFRS, prohibited US GAAP. Development costs: capitalized IFRS, expensed US GAAP. Investment property fair value: IFRS option.
options.d: 1) Identify contract. 2) Identify performance obligations. 3) Determine transaction price. 4) Allocate price to obligations. 5) Recognize revenue when/as obligation satisfied.

distractorExplanations.a: Every pair is reversed: LIFO is US GAAP only, write-down reversals and development-cost capitalization are IFRS treatments, and the fair value option for investment property is IFRS.
distractorExplanations.b: The frameworks still differ: IFRS bans LIFO, allows write-down reversals, capitalizes qualifying development costs, and offers a fair value model for investment property.
distractorExplanations.d: Revenue recognized when CONTROL transfers, not when cash received. Installment sales: recognize at sale if collectability probable.

options.a: Common stock (par value) + Additional paid-in capital (APIC) + Retained earnings + Accumulated other comprehensive income (AOCI) + Treasury stock added back as owner capital.
options.b: Common stock (par value) + Retained earnings + Current-year net income counted separately + Accumulated other comprehensive income (AOCI) - Dividends paid.
options.c: Common stock (par value) + Additional paid-in capital (APIC) + Retained earnings + Accumulated depreciation + Deferred tax liabilities - Treasury stock.
options.d: Common stock (par value) + Additional paid-in capital (APIC) + Retained earnings + Accumulated other comprehensive income (AOCI) - Treasury stock.

distractorExplanations.a: Sign error: treasury stock is a contra-equity account, so repurchased shares are subtracted from equity, not added.
distractorExplanations.b: Double counts net income, which already flows into retained earnings net of dividends, and omits APIC and treasury stock.
distractorExplanations.c: Accumulated depreciation is a contra-asset and deferred tax liabilities are liabilities; neither is a component of shareholders' equity.

options.a: EBIT = Earnings Before Interest and Tax = Operating Income. EBITDA adds back Depreciation and Amortization — proxy for operating cash flow.
options.b: Inventory turnover = COGS/Avg inventory. Receivables turnover = Revenue/Avg AR. Payables turnover = Purchases/Avg AP. Asset turnover = Revenue/Avg assets.
options.c: Current ratio = Current assets/Current liabilities. Quick ratio = (Cash + ST investments + Receivables)/CL. Cash ratio = Cash/CL.
options.d: Inventory turnover = Avg inventory/COGS. Receivables turnover = Avg AR/Revenue. Payables turnover = Avg AP/Purchases. Asset turnover = Avg assets/Revenue. Higher values mean faster conversion.

distractorExplanations.d: Each ratio is inverted: turnover puts the flow (COGS, revenue, purchases) in the numerator and the average balance in the denominator.
distractorExplanations.a: EBITDA ≠ cash flow (ignores working capital changes, capex). Useful for comparisons across capital structures. Widely used in leveraged buyout analysis.
distractorExplanations.c: Current ratio > 1 required for short-term solvency. Quick ratio removes illiquid inventory. Cash ratio most conservative. Industry context critical.

options.a: Basic EPS: net income / shares outstanding at year-end. Diluted EPS: assumes all options and convertibles are exercised, even antidilutive ones.
options.b: Basic EPS: net income / weighted average shares outstanding. Diluted EPS: assumes all dilutive securities (options, convertibles) exercised
options.c: Basic EPS: (net income + preferred dividends) / weighted average shares. Diluted EPS: same numerator, but excludes convertible securities from the share count.
options.d: Basic EPS: net income / weighted average shares including options. Diluted EPS: adds only convertible bonds, so it can exceed basic EPS.

distractorExplanations.a: Basic EPS uses weighted average shares, not year-end shares, and antidilutive securities are excluded from diluted EPS.
distractorExplanations.c: Preferred dividends are subtracted from net income, not added, and diluted EPS includes dilutive convertible securities.
distractorExplanations.d: Options belong in diluted EPS, not basic EPS, and diluted EPS can never exceed basic because antidilutive securities are excluded.

cfa-level-1-readiness-check-023.explanation: Basic EPS: net income / weighted average shares outstanding. Diluted EPS: assumes all dilutive securities (options, convertibles) exercised — always ≤ basic EPS. Formula: $$EPS_{basic} = \frac{NI - Preferred\ Div}{WASO}$$ Example: NI=$1M, preferred div=$100k, WASO=500k → Basic EPS=$1.80. Options add 50k shares (dilutive) → Diluted EPS = 900k/550k = $1.64. Diluted EPS is always ≤ basic EPS.

options.a: Without taxes: more debt raises firm value because debt is cheaper than equity. With taxes: debt adds no value since interest is not deductible. With distress costs: the optimal capital structure is 100% equity.
options.b: Without taxes: capital structure irrelevant, and the cost of equity stays flat as leverage rises. With taxes: debt raises WACC, so firms should avoid debt. With distress costs: higher leverage lowers expected distress costs.
options.c: Without taxes: firm value rises with leverage by t × D. With taxes: capital structure irrelevant because the tax shield is offset by a higher cost of equity. With distress costs: optimal leverage maximizes the tax shield alone.
options.d: Without taxes: capital structure irrelevant (firm value independent of leverage). With taxes: debt creates tax shield → optimal capital structure = 100% debt. With distress costs: optimal leverage balances tax shield vs distress costs.

distractorExplanations.a: Under M&M without taxes, cheaper debt is offset by a rising cost of equity so value is unchanged; interest is deductible, and distress costs imply an interior optimum, not 100% equity.
distractorExplanations.b: M&M Proposition II says the cost of equity rises with leverage; with taxes debt lowers WACC, and more leverage raises expected distress costs.
distractorExplanations.c: Swaps the propositions: the t × D tax shield appears only with taxes, while irrelevance holds without taxes; the trade-off balances the tax shield against distress costs.

options.a: For independent projects: NPV and IRR can give different accept/reject decisions. For mutually exclusive projects: IRR preferred when they conflict because it adjusts for project scale.
options.b: Conflicts arise only when projects have different discount rates. For mutually exclusive projects: choose the project with the shorter payback period when NPV and IRR disagree.
options.c: For independent projects: both give same accept/reject decision. For mutually exclusive projects: NPV preferred when conflict arises (different scale or timing of cash flows).
options.d: For independent projects: both give the same ranking. For mutually exclusive projects: IRR is preferred because it assumes reinvestment at the cost of capital.

distractorExplanations.a: Conventional independent projects get the same accept/reject decision from both; IRR ignores scale, which is why NPV wins when rankings conflict.
distractorExplanations.b: Conflicts come from differences in scale or cash-flow timing, and payback is not the tie-breaker; NPV is preferred.
distractorExplanations.d: IRR assumes reinvestment at the IRR itself; NPV assumes reinvestment at the cost of capital, which is one reason NPV is preferred.

options.a: Dividend irrelevance (M&M): investors prefer high-payout firms. Bird-in-hand: investors prefer capital gains because they are taxed later. Tax preference: investors prefer dividends since they are taxed at lower rates.
options.b: Signaling theory: dividend increases signal bad news. Clientele effect: investors all prefer the same payout policy. Residual dividend theory: firms pay dividends before funding positive-NPV projects.
options.c: Dividend irrelevance (M&M): dividend policy matters even in perfect markets. Bird-in-hand: dividends are riskier than capital gains. Tax preference: investors prefer dividends because capital gains taxes are paid immediately.
options.d: Dividend irrelevance (M&M): with perfect markets, dividend policy doesn't affect firm value. Bird-in-hand: investors prefer dividends (certain) over capital gains (uncertain). Tax preference: investors prefer capital gains (lower/deferred tax).

distractorExplanations.a: Mixes up the theories: irrelevance says payout does not matter, bird-in-hand favors dividends as more certain, and tax preference favors capital gains.
distractorExplanations.b: Dividend increases usually signal good news, clienteles differ in payout preference, and the residual approach pays dividends only after funding positive-NPV projects.
distractorExplanations.c: Irrelevance holds in perfect markets, bird-in-hand treats dividends as less risky than capital gains, and capital gains taxes are deferred until sale.

options.a: Calendar effects (December effect). Growth premium (high P/B outperforms). Size effect (large caps outperform). Momentum (recent winners reverse). Pre-earnings drift.
options.b: Calendar effects (January effect). Value premium (high P/E outperforms low P/E). Size effect (large caps outperform small caps). Mean reversion within days.
options.c: Calendar effects (January effect). Value premium (low P/B outperforms). Size effect (small caps outperform). Momentum (recent winners continue). Post-earnings drift.
options.d: Anomalies are pricing errors that persist after costs, proving markets are inefficient in the strong form only. Examples: insider trading profits, dividend signaling, and closed-end fund discounts.

distractorExplanations.a: Each anomaly is reversed: the documented effects are January, value (low P/B), small-cap outperformance, momentum continuation, and post-earnings drift.
distractorExplanations.b: The value premium refers to low P/E or low P/B stocks outperforming, and the size effect is small caps outperforming large caps.
distractorExplanations.d: Many anomalies disappear after costs or reflect risk, so they do not prove inefficiency, and insider trading profits test the strong form rather than being a market anomaly.

options.a: P/E divided by earnings growth rate — adjusts P/E for growth. PEG < 1 often considered undervalued.
options.b: Market price per share divided by book value per share. Leading uses next year's book value; trailing uses last year's.
options.c: Market price per share divided by earnings per share. Leading P/E uses next year's EPS. Trailing P/E uses last year's EPS.
options.d: Expected return of any asset = risk-free rate + beta × equity risk premium. Only systematic (market) risk is priced.

distractorExplanations.b: Dividing price by book value per share gives the P/B ratio; the P/E ratio divides price by earnings per share.
distractorExplanations.a: Growth rate should match P/E horizon (1-year forward). PEG oversimplifies — ignores risk, capital requirements, sustainability of growth.
distractorExplanations.d: CAPM uses EXPECTED returns, not historical. Idiosyncratic (company-specific) risk is NOT priced — can be diversified away.

options.a: Weak form: prices reflect all past trading data (technical analysis useless). Semi-strong: prices reflect all public info (fundamental analysis useless).
options.b: Efficient frontier when risk-free asset exists — all investors hold combination of risk-free asset and market portfolio.
options.c: Graphical representation of CAPM — plots expected return vs beta for all assets. Assets above SML = undervalued (positive alpha). Below SML = overvalued.
options.d: Borrowing from broker to buy securities. Initial margin: minimum equity at purchase. Maintenance margin: minimum equity to avoid margin call.

distractorExplanations.a: EMH doesn't say prices are correct — says they're unpredictable. Anomalies (momentum, value premium) are consistent with EMH if they reflect risk.
distractorExplanations.b: CML applies to EFFICIENT portfolios only. SML applies to ALL assets (efficient or not). CML uses total risk; SML uses beta.
distractorExplanations.d: Margin call trigger price = Loan / (1 - maintenance margin). At 30% maintenance: trigger = 5000/0.70 = $7,143.

options.a: Annual coupon divided by the bond's current market price. Ignores capital gain or loss to maturity and the time value of money.
options.b: Yield on a zero-coupon bond for a specific maturity — the pure time-value rate for that horizon. The building block of bond valuation.
options.c: IRR of bond's cash flows — discount rate that makes PV of all cash flows equal to current price. Assumes hold to maturity and reinvestment at YTM.
options.d: IRR of bond's cash flows using the coupon rate as the discount rate. Assumes coupons are reinvested at the coupon rate and the bond is sold at par before maturity.

distractorExplanations.a: Coupon divided by price is the current yield; YTM also captures the gain or loss to par and discounts all cash flows.
distractorExplanations.d: YTM is the rate that equates PV of cash flows to price, not the coupon rate; it assumes holding to maturity with reinvestment at the YTM.
distractorExplanations.b: Spot rates are bootstrapped from coupon bond prices. Each spot rate is unique to its maturity — unlike YTM which blends multiple periods.

options.a: Spot price minus futures price. Basis converges to zero at expiry. Basis risk: uncertainty about basis at time of hedge lifting.
options.b: Fundamental relationship between European call and put prices with same strike and expiry. Allows creation of synthetic positions.
options.c: Relationship between American call and put prices with any strike and expiry. Allows arbitrage whenever calls cost more than puts.
options.d: Futures: exchange-traded, standardized, daily mark-to-market (variation margin), centrally cleared (no counterparty risk). Forwards: OTC, customizable, settled at expiry, counterparty risk.

distractorExplanations.c: Put-call parity holds for European options with the same strike and expiry; calls costing more than puts is not by itself an arbitrage.
distractorExplanations.a: Basis is NOT zero (except at expiry). Hedger trades price risk for basis risk — basis risk is smaller and more predictable.
distractorExplanations.d: Daily settlement creates reinvestment effect — futures price ≠ forward price when rates are stochastic. Practically small difference.

options.a: Fundamental relationship between European call and put prices with same strike and expiry. Allows creation of synthetic positions.
options.b: Long stock + short call. Limits upside (call may be exercised) but generates premium income. Used when expecting flat to slightly up market.
options.c: Continuous trading, no transaction costs, constant volatility, lognormal returns, European option, known constant risk-free rate, no dividends.
options.d: Discrete trading, transaction costs included, volatility that changes with price, normally distributed prices, American options, and dividends paid continuously.

distractorExplanations.d: Reverses the BSM assumptions: continuous trading, no transaction costs, constant volatility, lognormal prices, and European options.
distractorExplanations.a: Put-call parity for EUROPEAN options only. American options can violate it due to early exercise. Rearrange to find any missing price.
distractorExplanations.b: Max profit = X - S₀ + C (capped at strike). Max loss = S₀ - C (reduced by premium). Breakeven = S₀ - C.

options.a: Excess return per unit of systematic risk (beta). Use for well-diversified portfolios or components of a larger portfolio.
options.b: Systematic (market/beta) risk: affects all assets, cannot be diversified away — rewarded with higher expected return. Unsystematic (idiosyncratic) risk: company-specific, diversifiable — NOT rewarded.
options.c: Excess return per unit of active risk (tracking error). Use to judge a manager's skill versus a benchmark.
options.d: Excess return per unit of total risk (standard deviation). Measures risk-adjusted performance for total portfolio.

distractorExplanations.c: Return per unit of tracking error is the information ratio; the Treynor ratio divides excess return by beta.
distractorExplanations.b: CAPM: only systematic risk is priced. Holding concentrated portfolio = bearing unrewarded idiosyncratic risk.
distractorExplanations.d: Sharpe uses TOTAL risk (σ). Treynor uses systematic risk (β). Information ratio uses active risk. Use Sharpe for total portfolio, Treynor for diversified component.

options.a: Set of portfolios with maximum expected return for each level of risk — or minimum risk for each return level.
options.b: Set of portfolios combining the risk-free asset with the market portfolio; its slope is the Sharpe ratio.
options.c: Portfolio with the lowest possible variance for given set of assets. Not necessarily the optimal portfolio.
options.d: Excess return per unit of total risk (standard deviation). Measures risk-adjusted performance for total portfolio.

distractorExplanations.b: Combining the risk-free asset with the market portfolio gives the capital market line, not the efficient frontier of risky assets.
distractorExplanations.c: Minimum variance ≠ maximum Sharpe ratio. Efficient frontier connects all minimum variance portfolios for each return level.
distractorExplanations.d: Sharpe uses TOTAL risk (σ). Treynor uses systematic risk (β). Information ratio uses active risk. Use Sharpe for total portfolio, Treynor for diversified component.

cfa-level-1-readiness-check-049.explanation: Set of portfolios with maximum expected return for each level of risk — or minimum risk for each return level. Rational investors choose only efficient portfolios. Formula: $$\text{Efficient: } E(R_p) \text{ maximized for given } \sigma_p$$ Example: Points on efficient frontier dominate all interior points. Adding a new asset with low correlation shifts frontier up-left (better risk-return). No rational investor holds interior portfolio. Rational investors choose only efficient portfolios.

options.a: Excess return per unit of total risk (standard deviation). Measures risk-adjusted performance for total portfolio.
options.b: Active return (vs benchmark) per unit of active risk (tracking error). Measures consistency of active management skill.
options.c: Diversification reduces risk only when correlation is negative. No benefit when correlation is between 0 and 1.
options.d: Diversification reduces portfolio risk whenever correlation < 1. Benefit increases as correlation decreases.

distractorExplanations.c: Any correlation below +1 lowers portfolio risk; negative correlation gives more benefit, but positive correlations below 1 still help.
distractorExplanations.a: Sharpe uses TOTAL risk (σ). Treynor uses systematic risk (β). Information ratio uses active risk. Use Sharpe for total portfolio, Treynor for diversified component.
distractorExplanations.b: IR measures active management. Sharpe measures total portfolio. A manager with IR=0.5 consistently adds 0.5% per unit of active risk taken.

cfa-level-1-readiness-check-050.explanation: Diversification reduces portfolio risk whenever correlation < 1. Benefit increases as correlation decreases. Maximum benefit when ρ = -1. Formula: $$\sigma_p < w_1\sigma_1 + w_2\sigma_2 \text{ when } \rho < 1$$ Example: Two assets, each σ=20%, ρ=0: σ_p = √(0.5²×400+0.5²×400) = 14.1% vs simple average 20%. Diversification saved 5.9%. Maximum benefit when ρ = -1.

options.a: Systematic risk: company-specific, can be diversified away — NOT rewarded. Unsystematic risk: market-wide, cannot be diversified away — rewarded with higher expected return.
options.b: Systematic (market/beta) risk: affects all assets, cannot be diversified away — rewarded with higher expected return. Unsystematic (idiosyncratic) risk: company-specific, diversifiable — NOT rewarded.
options.c: Systematic (market/beta) risk: affects all assets, can be eliminated with 30+ stocks — rewarded with a premium. Unsystematic (idiosyncratic) risk: company-specific, cannot be diversified away — also rewarded.
options.d: Diversification reduces portfolio risk whenever correlation < 1. Benefit increases as correlation decreases. Maximum benefit when ρ = -1.

distractorExplanations.a: The labels are swapped: systematic risk is market-wide and priced, while unsystematic risk is company-specific and diversifiable.
distractorExplanations.c: Holding 30+ stocks removes unsystematic risk, not systematic risk, and only systematic risk earns a premium.
distractorExplanations.d: Diversification eliminates UNSYSTEMATIC risk only. Systematic (market) risk cannot be diversified away no matter how many assets.

options.a: Cash available to ALL capital providers (debt + equity) after operating expenses and reinvestment. Discounted at WACC.
options.b: Weighted average time to receive bond's cash flows — weights are PV of each cash flow as proportion of bond price. Measured in years.
options.c: FIFO: newest costs in COGS, oldest in inventory. LIFO: oldest costs in COGS, newest in inventory (allowed under IFRS and US GAAP). WAC: average cost for all units.
options.d: FIFO: oldest costs in COGS, newest in inventory. LIFO: newest costs in COGS, oldest in inventory (US GAAP only). WAC: average cost for all units.

distractorExplanations.c: Swaps FIFO and LIFO cost flows and wrongly says IFRS allows LIFO; LIFO is permitted only under US GAAP.
distractorExplanations.a: FCFF discounted at WACC → firm value. Subtract debt → equity value. FCFE discounted at cost of equity → equity value directly.
distractorExplanations.b: Duration = maturity ONLY for zero-coupon bonds. Higher coupon → shorter duration. Higher YTM → shorter duration.
